library-fish-gills-tell-2: Most fish take it from water with gills.
library-fish-gills-tell-3: We use lungs to breathe air.
library-fish-gills-more-1: Water carries a small amount of dissolved oxygen.
library-fish-gills-more-2: A fish moves water over its gills, where oxygen passes into the blood.
library-fish-gills-more-3: The blood carries oxygen through the body.
library-fish-gills-more-4: Gills are delicate, so leave a fish in its watery home.
library-fish-gills-more-5: A fish is not splitting water into the gases that make it.
library-fish-gills-deep-1: Gills have many thin surfaces with blood flowing close to the water.
library-fish-gills-deep-2: This gives dissolved oxygen a short path into the blood and lets carbon dioxide move out.
library-fish-gills-deep-3: Many fish draw water in through the mouth and send it out past the gills.
library-fish-gills-deep-4: Moving water and blood keep gas exchange going.
library-fish-gills-deep-5: Gills and lungs solve a similar problem in different surroundings: bringing oxygen to living cells.
library-fish-gills-deep-6: Most fish rely on gills, but some have adaptations for taking oxygen from air as well.
library-fish-gills-deep-7: A turtle or dolphin coming to the surface is using lungs, not fish gills.
library-crab-shells-tell-1: A crab has a hard coat.
library-crab-shells-tell-2: It helps guard the soft parts inside.
library-crab-shells-tell-3: The crab sheds it as it grows.
library-crab-shells-more-1: A crab’s hard outer covering is called an exoskeleton.
library-crab-shells-more-2: It supports the body and helps protect it.
library-crab-shells-more-3: The hard covering cannot stretch enough for continued growth, so a crab molts: it leaves an old covering behind.
library-crab-shells-more-4: The new one is soft at first and then hardens.
library-crab-shells-more-5: A fresh molt can look like an empty crab.
library-crab-shells-deep-1: A crab makes its own exoskeleton; it is part of the animal’s body covering.
library-crab-shells-deep-2: Before a molt, changes beneath the old shell prepare a new covering.
library-crab-shells-deep-3: The crab backs out, expands while the new covering is soft, and later hardens it.
library-crab-shells-deep-4: This is a vulnerable time because the usual hard protection is missing.
library-crab-shells-deep-5: Different kinds and ages of crabs molt at different rates.
library-crab-shells-deep-6: A hermit crab’s borrowed snail shell is a separate shelter for its softer abdomen, not the exoskeleton it grows and molts.
library-crab-shells-deep-7: Do not pull a crab out of either kind of covering.
library-parrotfish-tell-2: Many scrape food from reef rock.
library-parrotfish-tell-3: Small bits of sand can come out too.
library-parrotfish-more-1: Parrotfish get their name from teeth that look a little like a bird’s beak.
library-parrotfish-more-2: Many kinds scrape or bite reef surfaces while feeding on algae and other tiny living material.
library-parrotfish-more-3: Some rock comes off with the food.
library-parrotfish-more-4: Grinding and digestion break it into smaller pieces, and the fish passes some of those pieces as sand.
library-parrotfish-deep-1: A reef surface holds a mixture of algae, microbes and material within the rock.
library-parrotfish-deep-2: Parrotfish feeding is more varied than saying that every parrotfish simply eats coral.
library-parrotfish-deep-3: Scraping and excavating species remove different amounts of reef material.
library-parrotfish-deep-4: Some swallowed calcium carbonate is ground and eventually released as sediment.
library-parrotfish-deep-5: This process is one contributor to sand on some tropical beaches, not an explanation for every grain on every beach.
library-parrotfish-deep-6: Grazing can also influence how much algae covers a reef.
library-parrotfish-deep-7: Parrotfish therefore connect feeding, reef surfaces and sand movement in the same living system.
library-tide-pool-label: Who lives in a tide pool?
library-tide-pool-tell-1: A tide pool holds sea water.
library-tide-pool-tell-2: Small plants and animals can live there.
library-tide-pool-more-1: When the tide goes out, water may stay in dips among coastal rocks.
library-tide-pool-more-2: These tide pools can shelter algae, crabs, snails and small fish, depending on the place.
library-tide-pool-more-3: The water can warm in the Sun and change as waves reach it.
library-tide-pool-more-4: A tide pool is a changing home, not a bowl of pets to take away.
library-tide-pool-deep-1: Tide-pool life must cope with changes between high and low tide.
library-tide-pool-deep-2: A pool can become warmer or saltier as water evaporates.
library-tide-pool-deep-4: When the tide rises, waves bring new seawater and animals may move in or out.
library-tide-pool-deep-5: Some residents cling to rocks or shelter in cracks.
library-tide-pool-deep-6: Which animals are present depends on the shore, the pool and the time; this picture is not a guaranteed Guam species list.
library-tide-pool-deep-7: Rocks can be slippery and waves can arrive suddenly.
library-tide-pool-deep-8: Choose a safe viewing place with a grown-up, without climbing down to reach an animal.
library-beach-sand-label: Where does beach sand come from?
library-beach-sand-tell-1: Sand is made of small grains.
library-beach-sand-tell-3: Some come from shells and reefs.
library-beach-sand-more-1: Waves and weather can break rock into small pieces.
library-beach-sand-more-2: Rivers and currents move those pieces.
library-beach-sand-more-3: On some warm-water beaches, broken shells and other hard parts of sea life also add grains.
library-beach-sand-more-4: Parrotfish can help make some reef sand.
library-beach-sand-more-5: A beach’s sand tells a story about nearby rocks, living things and moving water.
library-beach-sand-deep-1: Sand describes a grain-size range, rather than one single material.
library-beach-sand-deep-2: Two sandy beaches can therefore have different ingredients and colors.
library-beach-sand-deep-3: Quartz-rich rock can supply many grains; coral reefs and shells can supply calcium carbonate grains.
library-beach-sand-deep-4: Breaking down, transporting and sorting these materials takes time.
library-beach-sand-deep-5: Waves may carry grains along the shore, while storms can shift much larger amounts.
library-beach-sand-deep-6: A handful cannot tell the whole history without closer study.
library-beach-sand-deep-7: Our drawing enlarges a few grains to show possible sources and is not a microscope view of a particular Guam beach.
library-beach-sand-deep-8: Leave sand and shells where they belong.
library-mangrove-roots-tell-1: Mangroves are trees by the sea.
library-mangrove-roots-tell-2: Their roots can shelter small animals.
library-mangrove-roots-tell-3: They help hold muddy shore ground.
library-mangrove-roots-more-1: Mangroves grow along sheltered tropical and subtropical coasts.
library-mangrove-roots-more-2: They have ways to cope with salty water and wet, low-oxygen mud.
library-mangrove-roots-more-3: Roots can slow water and trap sediment.
library-mangrove-roots-more-4: Among the roots, young fish and other animals may find shelter.
library-mangrove-roots-more-5: There are different kinds of mangroves, and their roots do not all look alike.
library-mangrove-roots-deep-1: A mangrove forest joins land and sea rather than fitting neatly into only one.
library-mangrove-roots-deep-2: Its roots help stabilize sediments and reduce erosion in some coastal settings.
library-mangrove-roots-deep-3: Leaves and other organic material become part of a food web, while many animals use the sheltered space.
library-mangrove-roots-deep-4: Some mangroves have prop roots; others have roots that project above the mud and help gas exchange.
library-mangrove-roots-deep-5: Not every root is a drinking straw and not every mangrove removes salt the same way.
library-mangrove-roots-deep-6: Healthy mangroves can soften wave effects, but they cannot promise safety from every storm.
library-mangrove-roots-deep-7: Look from an established path with a grown-up.
library-jellyfish-move-tell-1: A jellyfish has a soft bell.
library-jellyfish-move-tell-2: It squeezes the bell to push water.
library-jellyfish-move-more-1: A jellyfish is an animal without bones.
library-jellyfish-move-more-2: By contracting its bell and then relaxing, it moves water and can swim.
library-jellyfish-move-more-3: Even swimming jellyfish drift with ocean currents.
library-jellyfish-move-more-4: The trailing tentacles help many kinds catch food; they are not legs for walking.
library-jellyfish-move-more-5: Watch jellyfish from a distance and never pick one up, even on the beach.
library-jellyfish-move-deep-1: The bell contains muscles that contract and change its shape.
library-jellyfish-move-deep-2: Water motion around the pulsing bell helps propel the jellyfish, but swimming ability differs among species.
library-jellyfish-move-deep-3: Currents still play an important part in where it goes.
library-jellyfish-move-deep-4: Jellyfish tentacles have specialized stinging cells used in feeding and defense.
library-jellyfish-move-deep-5: A stranded jellyfish or a loose tentacle can still pose a stinging risk.
library-jellyfish-move-deep-6: This drawing shows a simplified bell and a few tentacles, not a guide for deciding which animals are safe to touch.
library-jellyfish-move-deep-7: A jellyfish is not a fish: its body plan and way of moving are very different.
library-whale-song-tell-2: Sound can travel through sea water.
library-whale-song-tell-3: The songs help whales send signals.
library-whale-song-more-2: Males produce long, patterned songs, especially in breeding areas.
library-whale-song-more-3: Scientists study how those songs change and what they do.
library-whale-song-more-4: Singing is connected with reproduction, but its full role is still being explored.
library-whale-song-more-5: Not every whale species sings the same kind of song, and not every whale sound is a song.
library-whale-song-deep-1: A humpback song contains repeated sound units grouped into longer patterns.
library-whale-song-deep-2: Songs can change over time and can be shared among males in a population.
library-whale-song-deep-3: Researchers compare recordings to learn about behavior and connections between groups.
library-whale-song-deep-4: Sound can be useful where underwater visibility is limited.
library-whale-song-deep-5: However, a recording does not translate neatly into a human sentence such as hello or come here.
library-whale-song-deep-6: Scientists test explanations about attracting mates and interactions among males rather than claiming a complete whale dictionary.
library-whale-song-deep-7: Boat noise and other human-made sounds can affect the underwater sound environment.
library-whale-song-deep-8: Our illustration shows sound as curved lines; real sound waves are invisible.
library-guam-made-tell-2: Much of the north has limestone too.
library-guam-made-tell-3: Land and sea changed over time.
library-guam-made-more-1: Guam’s rocks record more than one kind of building.
library-guam-made-more-3: Sea life helped build limestone in shallow water.
library-guam-made-more-4: Earth movements and changing sea levels left some of that limestone above the sea.
library-guam-made-more-5: Today the north is largely a limestone plateau, while much of the south has volcanic hills.
library-guam-made-deep-1: Geologists read rock layers as evidence of earlier environments.
library-guam-made-deep-2: Southern Guam exposes several volcanic formations, while the north has thick limestone formations.
library-guam-made-deep-3: Limestone can include the hard remains of marine organisms and sediment formed in reef or lagoon settings.
library-guam-made-deep-4: Uplift and changes in sea level help explain why marine limestone now forms dry land.
library-guam-made-deep-5: This was a long, uneven history, not one volcano popping up as the island we see today.
library-guam-made-deep-6: Different rock types also affect water: rain can soak quickly into permeable northern limestone, while less permeable volcanic terrain supports more surface streams.
library-guam-made-deep-7: A rock map connects the island’s past with its water today.
library-limestone-tell-1: Limestone is a kind of rock.
library-limestone-tell-2: Many kinds hold bits from sea life.
library-limestone-tell-3: Some of Guam’s ground is limestone.
library-limestone-more-1: Corals, shells and other sea life can leave hard calcium carbonate parts behind.
library-limestone-more-2: Over time, such material can become limestone.
library-limestone-more-3: Much of northern Guam has limestone, including rock formed in old reef and lagoon settings.
library-limestone-more-4: Water can move through openings in it.
library-limestone-more-5: Not every limestone has visible shells, and limestone can form in other ways too.
library-limestone-deep-1: Limestone is a sedimentary rock made mainly of calcium carbonate.
library-limestone-deep-2: Some forms contain recognizable fossils, while others are made of very fine grains.
library-limestone-deep-3: Guam’s named limestone formations differ in age, texture and how they formed.
library-limestone-deep-4: Rainwater moving through cracks and pores can slowly dissolve limestone and enlarge openings.
library-limestone-deep-5: This helps explain why an aquifer can hold water within rock rather than in one giant underground tank.
library-limestone-deep-6: A small drawing of shells becoming rock skips burial, cementation and long spans of time.
library-limestone-deep-7: It also cannot identify a real rock by color alone.
library-limestone-deep-8: Leave rocks in place and avoid caves and unstable edges.
library-guam-rail-tell-1: The Guam rail is a bird.
library-guam-rail-tell-3: People work to help this rare bird.
library-guam-rail-more-1: The Guam rail is a small, mostly ground-living bird native to Guam.
library-guam-rail-more-2: Its wings are short and it is considered flightless.
library-guam-rail-more-3: Introduced brown treesnakes were a major cause of its loss from the wild on Guam.
library-guam-rail-more-4: Breeding and conservation work have helped keep the species from disappearing.
library-guam-rail-more-5: Watching wildlife kindly means giving it room.
library-guam-rail-deep-1: Rails use dense vegetation for cover as they search near the ground for food.
library-guam-rail-deep-2: The Guam rail evolved on an island without the introduced brown treesnake.
library-guam-rail-deep-3: When snakes spread, many native birds faced predation they were poorly equipped to escape.
library-guam-rail-deep-4: Conservation breeding and carefully managed releases have been important parts of helping the rail.
library-guam-rail-deep-5: Habitat protection and control of introduced predators are also needed; simply opening a cage is not a recovery plan.
library-guam-rail-deep-6: Conservation status and release populations change, so this draft does not give a current population count or promise that a rail lives at a particular walking spot.
library-guam-rail-deep-7: The picture is an original simplified bird, not identification evidence.
library-limestone-forest-tell-1: A forest can grow on limestone.
library-limestone-forest-tell-2: Roots reach into soil and cracks.
library-limestone-forest-tell-3: Leaves make shade for life below.
library-limestone-forest-more-1: Parts of Guam support forest on limestone ground.
library-limestone-forest-more-2: Trees, vines and other plants make a layered home for animals.
library-limestone-forest-more-3: Thin soil and openings in the rock affect where roots can grow and how water moves.
library-limestone-forest-more-4: A forest is more than a group of tall trees: smaller plants, seedlings and soil life matter too.
library-limestone-forest-deep-1: A limestone forest is named for the ground beneath it, not for trees made of stone.
library-limestone-forest-deep-2: Rock, soil, rainfall and living things interact.
library-limestone-forest-deep-3: Plants provide food and shelter, and new seedlings help a forest renew itself.
library-limestone-forest-deep-4: On Guam, introduced animals and invasive plants can disrupt those connections.
library-limestone-forest-deep-5: Restoration work includes choosing suitable native plants and managing threats, rather than simply planting any fast-growing tree.
library-limestone-forest-deep-6: A recovering forest may need ongoing care.
library-limestone-forest-deep-7: This illustration combines plant shapes to show layers; it is not a list of species that must grow together.
library-limestone-forest-deep-8: Follow established paths with a grown-up and leave plants where they are.
library-drinking-water-label: Where does our drinking water come from?
library-drinking-water-tell-1: Rain helps fill our water supply.
library-drinking-water-tell-3: People collect and treat water for us.
library-drinking-water-more-1: Much of Guam’s water supply comes from wells in the northern limestone aquifer.
library-drinking-water-more-2: An aquifer is rock or sediment that holds and passes groundwater.
library-drinking-water-more-3: Rain soaks down to refill it.
library-drinking-water-more-5: Water-system workers treat and check drinking water.
library-drinking-water-more-6: Clear-looking stream, well or rainwater is not automatically safe to drink.
library-drinking-water-deep-1: Fresh groundwater in northern Guam forms a lens above denser salty water, with a mixing zone between them.
library-drinking-water-deep-2: It fills spaces within limestone; it is not one hollow lake.
library-drinking-water-deep-3: Rainfall, pumping and ocean conditions affect this system.
library-drinking-water-deep-4: Surface runoff is more common on the south’s less permeable volcanic terrain, where streams and reservoirs also supply water.
library-drinking-water-deep-5: Protecting the land above an aquifer helps protect the water below because contaminants can move down with infiltrating water.
library-drinking-water-deep-6: The older USGS source explains the physical system, not today’s water-quality alerts.
library-drinking-water-deep-7: Ask a grown-up to follow the water provider’s current guidance rather than using this page to decide if a tap is safe.
library-village-tell-2: People live and do things there.
library-village-tell-3: Each village has its own stories.
library-village-more-2: A village can include homes, roads, shared places and people who help their neighbors.
library-village-more-3: Villages have different histories and may change over time.
library-village-more-4: A map shows boundaries, but it cannot show every friendship, family memory or way of belonging.
library-village-more-5: Ask a grown-up about a place that matters to your family.
library-village-deep-1: A village is both a place and a community of people.
library-village-deep-2: On Guam, village names and boundaries help people describe where they live and organize local services.
library-village-deep-3: A simple map can show location, while people’s accounts explain lived experiences that a map leaves out.
library-village-deep-4: No single picture of a building, meal or celebration represents every resident.
library-village-deep-5: Families may have connections with several villages and with places beyond Guam.
library-village-deep-6: Listening respectfully means allowing people to describe their own community rather than treating one story as the only story.
library-village-deep-7: This page gives no invented traditional practice or translated village name.
library-village-deep-8: People who live in a place can help check how its story is told.
library-native-trees-tell-1: Native trees belong in a place’s long story.
library-native-trees-tell-2: They can give local animals food and shelter.
library-native-trees-tell-3: Young trees help a forest grow.
library-native-trees-more-1: A native tree is part of a region’s naturally occurring plant life.
library-native-trees-more-2: Native plants can provide food and shelter that local animals use.
library-native-trees-more-3: On Guam, restoring limestone forest includes growing appropriate native plants and reducing threats.
library-native-trees-more-4: A tree is not helpful just because it grows fast.
library-native-trees-more-5: Good restoration pays attention to the whole place.
library-native-trees-deep-1: Native does not mean that an individual tree never moves or changes.
library-native-trees-deep-2: It describes a species’ history in a region, rather than a person’s identity.
library-native-trees-deep-3: Forest recovery depends on relationships among seedlings, mature plants, animals, soil and water.
library-native-trees-deep-4: Invasive vines can crowd other plants, and introduced animals can change which seedlings survive.
library-native-trees-deep-5: Restoration teams choose plants for the habitat and manage those pressures.
library-native-trees-deep-6: Removing threats and supporting natural regrowth can matter alongside planting.
library-native-trees-deep-7: This page does not identify any tree from its leaf shape or tell a child which plant to remove.
library-native-trees-deep-8: Local experts and land managers guide that work.
library-native-trees-deep-9: A family can watch growth without taking leaves or seeds.
library-family-walk-label: What can we notice on a family walk?
library-family-walk-tell-2: Look for shapes, shade and small changes.
library-family-walk-tell-3: You can draw what you see.
library-family-walk-more-1: A familiar path can hold new details: a leaf’s edge, a shadow, a bird far away or rainwater moving downhill.
library-family-walk-more-2: Choose an established route with a grown-up and leave wildlife and plants in place.
library-family-walk-more-3: Familia is a CHamoru word for family.
library-family-walk-more-4: A family’s walk can become a page of observations rather than a hunt for prizes.
library-family-walk-deep-1: An observation records what you notice, while an explanation proposes why it happens.
library-family-walk-deep-2: You might draw wet ground under a tree, then wonder whether rain fell there or water dripped from leaves.
library-family-walk-deep-3: Revisit safely with a grown-up to compare, without disturbing the place.
library-family-walk-deep-4: Dates and drawings can help show change; a photograph or guess alone may not identify a species.
library-family-walk-deep-5: People experience places in different ways, and a short accessible route can offer as much to notice as a long hike.
library-family-walk-deep-6: Families can choose which languages and stories to share together.
library-family-walk-deep-7: Invite your family’s own account of the place instead of inventing a tradition for it.
library-distant-stars-tell-2: They look like dots from here.
library-distant-stars-more-1: The Sun is a star, but it is much closer than the other stars we see at night.
library-distant-stars-more-2: A faraway thing takes up a smaller part of our view.
library-distant-stars-more-3: That is why a giant star can look like a tiny point.
library-distant-stars-more-4: How bright it looks also depends on how much light it gives off, not just its distance.
library-distant-stars-deep-1: A star’s apparent size is how wide it looks from our viewpoint; its actual size is the size of the star itself.
library-distant-stars-deep-3: Astronomers use measurements rather than the size of a dot in a drawing to compare stars.
library-distant-stars-deep-4: Brightness is another clue, but a bright-looking star might be close or might give off a great deal of light.
library-distant-stars-deep-5: A light-year measures distance: how far light travels in one year.
library-distant-stars-deep-6: It is not a star’s age.
library-distant-stars-deep-7: Light from distant stars takes years to reach us.
library-distant-stars-deep-8: Our star dots are symbols, greatly enlarged so that you can choose them.
library-shadow-tell-2: A shadow forms behind the thing in its way.
library-shadow-tell-3: Move the thing and the shadow can change.
library-shadow-more-1: A solid object can stop light from reaching part of a surface.
library-shadow-more-2: That darker area is a shadow.
library-shadow-more-3: Its shape and size depend on the positions of the light, object and surface.
library-shadow-more-4: A shadow is not a stain or a separate object.
library-shadow-more-5: With a grown-up, you can explore using a small flashlight aimed away from eyes.
library-shadow-deep-1: In a simple model, light travels in straight paths from a source.
library-shadow-deep-2: An opaque object blocks some of those paths, leaving an area that receives less light from that source.
library-shadow-deep-3: A wider light source can make a fuzzy edge because some light reaches around the object from other parts of the source.
library-shadow-deep-4: Moving the object closer to a flashlight can make its shadow larger on a fixed wall.
library-shadow-deep-5: Outdoor shadows change as the Sun’s position appears to change during Earth’s turn.
library-shadow-deep-6: This does not mean the Sun circles Earth each day.
library-shadow-deep-7: Never use the Sun or a bright beam as something to stare into.
library-constellation-tell-1: Stars can seem to make a shape.
library-constellation-tell-3: The lines are in our minds.
library-constellation-more-1: A constellation can help us describe a part of the sky.
library-constellation-more-2: The stars in a familiar pattern are not joined by real lines.
library-constellation-more-3: They may be at very different distances from Earth.
library-constellation-more-4: People in different cultures have seen and named different patterns.
library-constellation-more-5: Astronomers now use eighty-eight official constellation regions to map the sky.
library-constellation-deep-1: The everyday picture of a constellation and the modern map region are related but not identical.
library-constellation-deep-2: A recognizable pattern can sit within a larger officially named region.
library-constellation-deep-3: Seen from Earth, unrelated stars may line up into a shape even though they are far apart in three-dimensional space.
library-constellation-deep-4: The patterns visible to you depend on your location, the season and the hour.
library-constellation-deep-5: Our exhibit uses an invented pattern to explain this idea and is not a guide to finding a named constellation above Guam tonight.
library-constellation-deep-6: We do not add a local traditional star story without a source and cultural review.
library-constellation-deep-7: You can freely invent your own picture and label it as invented.
library-night-view-label: Why does the sky look different at night?
library-night-view-tell-2: At night we face away from the Sun.
library-night-view-tell-3: Stars can stand out in the darker sky.
library-night-view-more-1: The Sun’s light makes the daytime sky bright, so most stars are hard to see.
library-night-view-more-2: Stars are still there in daytime.
library-night-view-more-3: During a night, Earth’s turn makes stars appear to move across our view.
library-night-view-more-4: Across the year, Earth’s trip around the Sun changes which direction the night side faces, so different stars can be visible.
library-night-view-deep-1: Three kinds of change can affect a night view.
library-night-view-deep-2: Earth’s rotation changes the view over hours; its orbit changes the night-facing direction over months; and your location on Earth changes how much of the sky is above your horizon.
library-night-view-deep-3: Clouds, nearby lights and the Moon’s brightness also affect what you can notice.
library-night-view-deep-4: A model that advances one step is choosing a view for learning, not speeding up the real sky or predicting tonight’s clouds.
library-night-view-deep-5: Stars have their own motions, but the familiar sweep during one night mainly comes from our turning viewpoint.
library-night-view-deep-6: Stargaze only with a grown-up from a safe place, away from roads and water edges.
library-telescope-tell-2: It helps us see faraway things.
library-telescope-tell-3: Never point one at the Sun.
library-telescope-more-1: A telescope uses shaped mirrors or lenses to collect and focus light.
library-telescope-more-2: More gathered light can reveal dim things that our eyes miss.
library-telescope-more-3: It is not a tube that brings stars closer to Earth.
library-telescope-more-4: Some telescopes record images with cameras.
library-telescope-more-5: A grown-up must help choose a safe target, because looking at the Sun through optics can damage eyes.
library-telescope-deep-1: The light-gathering surface of a telescope is its aperture.
library-telescope-deep-2: A larger aperture collects more light, while carefully shaped optics form an image.
library-telescope-deep-3: Magnification can make that image appear larger, but magnifying a blurry image does not create missing detail.
library-telescope-deep-4: Air turbulence, the quality of the optics and the kind of light being observed also matter.
library-telescope-deep-5: Some telescopes observe kinds of light our eyes cannot see, and their data can be displayed as images with explained colors.
library-telescope-deep-6: A space telescope avoids much of the blurring and absorption caused by Earth’s atmosphere.
library-telescope-deep-7: Our simple drawing shows an optical telescope, not every kind of astronomical instrument.
library-milky-way-tell-1: Our Sun is one star in a huge group.
library-milky-way-tell-2: That group is the Milky Way galaxy.
library-milky-way-more-1: A galaxy is a vast system of stars, gas, dust and other matter held together by gravity.
library-milky-way-more-2: Our solar system is part of the Milky Way, a barred spiral galaxy.
library-milky-way-more-3: On a dark night, part of its star-filled disk can look like a pale band across the sky.
library-milky-way-more-4: That band is not a cloud in Earth’s air.
library-milky-way-deep-1: We cannot travel outside the Milky Way to take its portrait.
library-milky-way-deep-2: Astronomers infer its shape from observations made within it, including maps of stars and gas.
library-milky-way-deep-3: The solar system is in the disk, away from the center.
library-milky-way-deep-4: Looking along the disk means looking through many distant stars; their combined light helps make the milky band.
library-milky-way-deep-5: Interstellar dust hides some visible light, so other wavelengths help reveal structure.
library-milky-way-deep-6: A spiral drawing in a book is therefore a model informed by evidence, not a photograph taken from above our galaxy.
library-milky-way-deep-7: Our solar system is just a small part of this much larger structure.
library-comet-tell-1: A comet is a small icy world.
library-comet-tell-2: Near the Sun, it can grow a glowing cloud and tails.
library-comet-more-1: A comet’s solid center contains ice, dust and rocky material.
library-comet-more-2: As it nears the Sun, warming lets gas and dust escape.
library-comet-more-3: These can form a cloud around the center and long tails.
library-comet-more-4: A comet travels around the Sun.
library-comet-more-5: Its tail does not simply point backward like a moving animal’s tail; sunlight and the solar wind affect it.
library-comet-deep-1: The solid center is called the nucleus, and the surrounding cloud is the coma.
library-comet-deep-2: A comet can have a dust tail and an ion tail, shaped differently by sunlight and the solar wind.
library-comet-deep-3: The ion tail generally points away from the Sun, so a comet moving away from the Sun can travel with that tail ahead of it.
library-comet-deep-4: Far from the Sun, a comet may be faint and show little visible activity.
library-comet-deep-5: A comet is different from a meteor, the streak of light produced when a small incoming object heats the atmosphere.
library-comet-deep-6: Our bright-tail drawing enlarges the tail and nucleus for recognition; it is not a scale diagram.
library-astronaut-home-label: How do astronauts live in space?
library-astronaut-home-tell-1: Astronauts need air, water and food.
library-astronaut-home-tell-3: They work, rest and exercise there.
library-astronaut-home-more-1: Inside a space station, equipment maintains air and manages water.
library-astronaut-home-more-2: Astronauts secure loose things so they do not drift away.
library-astronaut-home-more-3: They sleep in secured sleeping bags and use exercise equipment to help care for bones and muscles.
library-astronaut-home-more-4: Floating does not mean that gravity has vanished: the station and crew are falling around Earth together.
library-astronaut-home-deep-1: An orbiting station moves forward fast enough that its continuous fall follows Earth’s curve.
library-astronaut-home-deep-2: This shared free fall creates the apparent weightlessness called microgravity.
library-astronaut-home-deep-3: Life-support systems control important conditions inside the station, while crew members follow work, rest and maintenance routines.
library-astronaut-home-deep-4: Water recovery can reduce how much new water must be brought from Earth, but systems still need checking and supplies.
library-astronaut-home-deep-5: Exercise is important because muscles and bones experience different loads from those on the ground.
library-astronaut-home-deep-6: A spacesuit is needed for work outside the protected cabin.
library-astronaut-home-deep-7: This page describes life aboard an orbiting station, not every mission or a promise that humans can live unprotected anywhere in space.
library-breathing-tell-1: We breathe air in and out.
library-breathing-tell-2: Our lungs help oxygen reach our blood.
library-breathing-more-1: Air goes into the lungs when we breathe in.
library-breathing-more-2: Oxygen from the air passes into the blood, which carries it to cells around the body.
library-breathing-more-3: Carbon dioxide moves from the blood into the lungs and leaves when we breathe out.
library-breathing-more-4: Muscles help the chest change size so air can move.
library-breathing-more-5: You can let your breathing happen naturally.
library-breathing-deep-1: Tiny air sacs in the lungs, called alveoli, sit beside small blood vessels.
library-breathing-deep-2: Their thin walls allow gas exchange: oxygen enters blood and carbon dioxide leaves it.
library-breathing-deep-3: The diaphragm is a muscle beneath the lungs.
library-breathing-deep-4: When it contracts and moves downward, space in the chest increases and air flows in.
library-breathing-deep-5: When it relaxes, air can flow out.
library-breathing-deep-6: The brain usually adjusts breathing without a conscious plan, responding to the body’s needs.
library-breathing-deep-7: Lungs do not create oxygen, and breathing is not a contest for the longest pause.
library-breathing-deep-8: People may use different supports to breathe.
library-breathing-deep-9: This diagram explains a common process, not a test of anyone’s health.
library-heart-tell-2: It sends blood through your body.
library-heart-tell-3: Blood carries things your cells need.
library-heart-more-1: The heart is made largely of muscle.
library-heart-more-2: It squeezes and relaxes to move blood.
library-heart-more-3: Blood travels to the lungs to exchange gases, then to the body to deliver oxygen and nutrients.
library-heart-more-4: Valves help it move in the right direction.
library-heart-more-5: The familiar heart symbol is a drawing; the real organ has a different shape.
library-heart-deep-2: The right side sends blood toward the lungs, and the left side sends oxygen-rich blood toward the body.
library-heart-deep-3: Blood returning from the body begins the circuit again.
library-heart-deep-4: Small vessels let materials move between blood and tissues.
library-heart-deep-5: Valves reduce backward flow, while an electrical signaling system coordinates the muscle’s contractions.
library-heart-deep-6: The rate changes with activity and other needs, so there is no single speed that every child must match.
library-heart-deep-7: Our two-color arrows separate the routes for learning; blood is not blue inside a person.
library-heart-deep-8: This is a model of circulation, not an instruction to measure or judge a heartbeat.
library-bones-label: How do our bones help us?
library-bones-tell-3: Bones and muscles work together to move us.
library-bones-more-1: Your skeleton is a living framework.
library-bones-more-2: The skull surrounds the brain, and the ribs help protect organs in the chest.
library-bones-more-3: Many bones meet at joints, where movement can happen.
library-bones-more-4: Bone is not dry, dead material inside you: it grows and is renewed.
library-bones-more-5: Children’s bones change as their bodies grow.
library-bones-deep-1: Bone combines a strong mineral-containing structure with living cells and a protein framework.
library-bones-deep-2: It is continually remodeled as some tissue is removed and new tissue is made.
library-bones-deep-3: Bones support the body, protect organs and provide attachment points for muscles.
library-bones-deep-4: Marrow inside certain bones makes blood cells.
library-bones-deep-5: Cartilage and other tissues help joints work; a skeleton alone cannot move itself.
library-bones-deep-6: People’s bodies and movement supports differ, and a picture of one skeleton is not a standard everyone must fit.
library-bones-deep-7: Food, activity suited to the person and healthcare all play roles in bone health.
library-bones-deep-8: This page gives no diet, supplement or exercise prescription.
library-muscles-tell-2: Many pull on bones to move us.
library-muscles-more-1: Many muscles attach to bones through strong tissues called tendons.
library-muscles-more-2: When a muscle contracts, it can pull a bone at a joint.
library-muscles-more-3: Muscles often work in groups: some pull one way and others help move back or steady the joint.
library-muscles-more-4: The heart is muscle too, but it works differently from the muscles that bend an arm.
library-muscles-deep-1: Skeletal muscle contains fibers that can shorten and produce force.
library-muscles-deep-2: A tendon transfers that force to bone, and a joint allows a movement determined by its structure.
library-muscles-deep-3: Muscles can also hold tension without making a large visible movement, helping maintain posture or stabilize a joint.
library-muscles-deep-4: The nervous system coordinates which fibers work and when.
library-muscles-deep-5: Smooth muscle moves material within organs, while cardiac muscle makes the heart pump.
library-muscles-deep-6: These muscle types do not all wait for a deliberate decision.
library-muscles-deep-7: Movement can look different for different people, and tools or mobility supports may help.
library-muscles-deep-8: Our arm drawing simplifies a group of tissues into two pulling bands; it is not an exercise guide.
library-vision-tell-2: Cells send signals to the brain.
library-vision-tell-3: The brain helps us make sense of what we see.
library-vision-more-1: The clear front of an eye and its lens help focus light onto the retina at the back.
library-vision-more-2: Special cells there respond to light.
library-vision-more-3: Signals travel along the optic nerve to the brain.
library-vision-more-4: Seeing involves both eyes and brain; eyes do not shine a beam out at the world.
library-vision-more-5: People use different ways to explore when sight differs.
library-vision-deep-1: The cornea bends incoming light, and the lens helps focus it on the light-sensitive retina.
library-vision-deep-2: The pupil is an opening; the iris changes its size to regulate how much light enters.
library-vision-deep-3: Photoreceptor cells turn light into electrical signals.
library-vision-deep-4: The optic nerve carries those signals toward the brain, which uses them to construct visual experience.
library-vision-deep-5: This is not a tiny finished photograph being passed through a wire.
library-vision-deep-6: Many parts must work together, and glasses or other supports may help people use their vision.
library-vision-deep-7: An eye drawing cannot diagnose a problem.
library-vision-deep-8: Never stare at the Sun or shine bright lights into anyone’s eyes for an experiment.
library-hearing-tell-1: Sound can make parts of an ear move.
library-hearing-tell-2: Tiny cells turn that motion into signals.
library-hearing-more-1: Sound waves travel through the ear canal and vibrate the eardrum.
library-hearing-more-2: Small bones pass the vibrations on to a fluid-filled part of the inner ear.
library-hearing-more-3: Sensory cells there help make electrical signals.
library-hearing-more-4: A nerve carries them to the brain.
library-hearing-more-5: People hear in different ways and may use hearing devices, signs or other communication supports.
library-hearing-deep-1: The three small middle-ear bones transfer vibrations toward the cochlea, a curled structure in the inner ear.
library-hearing-deep-2: Waves in its fluid move a membrane and the sensory hair cells on it.
library-hearing-deep-3: Bending tiny projections on these cells helps create electrical signals.
library-hearing-deep-4: Different places along the cochlea respond to different sound frequencies.
library-hearing-deep-5: The auditory nerve carries information to the brain; no little voice travels down a hollow nerve.
library-hearing-deep-6: Loud sounds can harm hearing, so the model needs no loud-noise test.
library-hearing-deep-7: Our spiral is an enlarged symbol of the cochlea, and the drawn wave is a way to represent invisible vibration.
library-smell-tell-1: Tiny bits from some things reach our nose.
library-smell-tell-3: The brain can recognize a smell.
library-smell-more-1: Odor molecules can travel through air to a small patch of sensory cells high inside the nose.
library-smell-more-2: Receptors on these cells respond, and signals reach the brain.
library-smell-more-3: Smell also helps shape food’s flavor.
library-smell-more-4: People do not all smell the same things in the same way.
library-smell-more-5: Never sniff an unknown liquid, powder or plant to identify it.
library-smell-deep-1: The sensory cells used for smell are called olfactory neurons.
library-smell-deep-2: Molecules stimulate combinations of receptors, and the resulting pattern of signals helps the brain recognize an odor.
library-smell-deep-3: Aromas can reach these cells through the nostrils or from the mouth through a passage at the back of the throat while eating.
library-smell-deep-4: That connection helps explain why food can seem different when the nose is blocked.
library-smell-deep-5: Smell is one source of information, not a safety test: a pleasant odor does not prove a substance is safe, and some hazards have little smell.
library-smell-deep-6: This page asks for a drawing from memory rather than a sniffing experiment.
library-taste-tell-2: They send signals to the brain.
library-taste-more-1: Molecules from food can reach taste cells in the mouth.
library-taste-more-2: These cells respond to tastes such as sweet, sour, salty, bitter and savory.
library-taste-more-4: Flavor also includes smell, temperature and texture.
library-taste-more-5: A tongue is not divided into separate sweet and salty zones.
library-taste-more-6: You do not need to taste anything to explore this page.
library-taste-deep-1: Taste cells are grouped in taste buds, including many on the tongue.
library-taste-deep-2: Different types of cells respond to basic taste qualities, and they are spread across the tongue rather than confined to the familiar but misleading tongue map.
library-taste-deep-3: Umami is a name for a savory taste.
library-taste-deep-4: Smell receptors contribute information about aromas, while other nerves convey temperature, texture or sensations such as chili’s burning feeling.
library-taste-deep-5: The brain combines these signals into flavor.
library-taste-deep-6: Tastes and food needs differ among people, and an unfamiliar taste cannot prove food is safe.
library-taste-deep-7: Our drawing shows enlarged taste buds as symbols, not bumps that a child should count or test.
library-wheel-tell-2: It helps us move a load.
library-wheel-tell-3: A rod called an axle can help hold it.
library-wheel-more-1: Pulling a load across a surface means sliding it.
library-wheel-more-2: Wheels can let a cart roll instead, often reducing the force needed on a firm, level path.
library-wheel-more-3: Axles support or turn with wheels, depending on the design.
library-wheel-more-4: A wheel still needs a push or another source of energy.
library-wheel-more-5: It does not make a heavy load weightless.
library-wheel-deep-1: A wheel and axle can work as a simple machine.
library-wheel-deep-2: In one arrangement, turning a large wheel turns a smaller shaft, trading distance moved for turning force.
library-wheel-deep-3: A cart also uses rolling to reduce the resistance that sliding a load would create.
library-wheel-deep-4: These are related uses, but not exactly the same explanation.
library-wheel-deep-5: Real wheels lose energy through friction and deformation.
library-wheel-deep-6: Soft sand, an uneven path or a steep slope can make rolling harder.
library-wheel-deep-7: Engineers choose wheel size, material and bearings for the job.
library-wheel-deep-8: Our small cart model omits those details and does not claim that every wheeled object is easy or safe for a child to push.
library-lever-tell-1: A lever is a stiff bar.
library-lever-tell-3: A push at one end can lift the other.
library-lever-more-1: A seesaw is one kind of lever.
library-lever-more-2: The support it turns around is called a fulcrum.
library-lever-more-3: Where you push, where the load sits and where the fulcrum sits all matter.
library-lever-more-4: In some arrangements, pushing farther from the fulcrum lets a smaller force lift a load through a shorter distance.
library-lever-more-5: The lever does not create energy.
library-lever-deep-1: A turning effect depends on both force and distance from the pivot.
library-lever-deep-2: For a balanced simple lever, a smaller force farther from the pivot can balance a larger force closer to it.
library-lever-deep-3: When the lever moves, the end traveling farther trades that distance for force at the load.
library-lever-deep-4: Not every lever makes the needed input force smaller: other layouts help with speed or reach.
library-lever-deep-5: Real levers bend a little and have friction, so a perfect diagram leaves some effects out.
library-lever-deep-6: Our bar and triangle are a model, not instructions for lifting furniture or putting fingers near a pinch point.
library-lever-deep-7: Make a drawing rather than trying a heavy lift.
library-ramp-label: How does a ramp help us lift?
library-ramp-tell-1: A ramp is a sloping path.
library-ramp-tell-2: It can help move a load up.
library-ramp-tell-3: A gentler ramp takes a longer path.
library-ramp-more-1: A ramp is also called an inclined plane.
library-ramp-more-2: Instead of lifting a load straight up, you can move it along the slope.
library-ramp-more-3: For the same height, a longer, gentler ramp can reduce the force needed along the ramp.
library-ramp-more-4: You trade less force for more distance.
library-ramp-more-5: Friction still matters, and the load still needs energy to rise.
library-ramp-deep-1: In an ideal model without friction, raising the same load through the same vertical height takes the same amount of work whether the path is vertical or sloped.
library-ramp-deep-2: A gentle ramp spreads that work over a longer distance, reducing the force along the path.
library-ramp-deep-3: In the real world, friction and the kind of wheels or surface change the required effort.
library-ramp-deep-4: The slope also affects control on the way down.
library-ramp-deep-5: Ramps can improve access, but a drawing cannot establish that a real ramp is accessible or safe.
library-ramp-deep-6: Do not test a slope with a wheelchair, bicycle or heavy load; design a paper model instead.
library-gears-tell-2: Teeth on one can push another.
library-gears-tell-3: Two touching gears turn opposite ways.
library-gears-more-1: When two ordinary external gears mesh, their teeth fit into the gaps between each other.
library-gears-more-2: Turning one pushes the other around.
library-gears-more-3: If the gears have different numbers of teeth, they turn at different rates.
library-gears-more-4: A small gear must turn more times to turn a larger one once.
library-gears-more-5: Keep fingers away from real moving gears.
library-gears-deep-1: For meshing gears, the teeth passing the contact point must match, so the ratio of tooth counts sets the ratio of rotation rates.
library-gears-deep-2: If a driving gear has half as many teeth as the driven gear, it turns twice for each turn of the driven gear.
library-gears-deep-3: In an ideal system, slower output can provide more turning force, called torque.
library-gears-deep-5: A third gear placed between two external gears changes which direction the final one turns relative to the first.
library-gears-deep-7: Our diagram shows only a simple external pair; it is not a plan for operating machinery.
library-pulley-tell-1: A pulley has a wheel and rope.
library-pulley-tell-2: It can change a pull’s direction.
library-pulley-tell-3: Some pulley sets make lifting easier.
library-pulley-more-1: A rope runs around a pulley’s grooved wheel.
library-pulley-more-2: A fixed pulley can let you pull down to raise something up.
library-pulley-more-3: That change of direction does not by itself cut the force in half.
library-pulley-more-4: A system with moving pulleys can share the load among several rope sections.
library-pulley-more-5: Then a longer pull can raise the load with less force.
library-pulley-deep-1: Count the rope sections supporting a moving load in a simple ideal pulley system.
library-pulley-deep-2: More supporting sections can reduce the input force, but more rope must be pulled for the same rise.
library-pulley-deep-3: This is another trade between force and distance.
library-pulley-deep-4: A single fixed pulley mainly redirects the force; a moving pulley changes how the load is supported.
library-pulley-deep-5: Real systems also need force to overcome friction and move the pulley parts.
library-pulley-deep-6: The rope tension and anchoring must be safe, which a simple drawing cannot guarantee.
library-pulley-deep-7: Our picture is for tracing a force path, not a suggestion to hoist objects, hang ropes or make a climbing system.
library-boats-float-tell-1: Water pushes up on a boat.
library-boats-float-tell-2: A floating boat pushes water aside.
library-boats-float-tell-3: Its shape helps it hold up its load.
library-boats-float-more-1: A boat has weight pulling down, while the water exerts an upward buoyant force.
library-boats-float-more-2: A hollow hull can move aside a lot of water without having a large average density.
library-boats-float-more-3: That is why a boat made partly from heavy metal can float.
library-boats-float-more-4: It does not float because metal stops being heavy, and a boat can still sink.
library-boats-float-deep-1: Archimedes’ principle relates the buoyant force to the weight of displaced fluid.
library-boats-float-deep-2: A floating boat settles until the upward force balances its weight, including its load.
library-boats-float-deep-3: Hull shape makes space that can remain largely filled with air, lowering the average density of the boat and its contents.
library-boats-float-deep-4: Adding load makes the hull sit lower and displace more water, up to its safe limits.
library-boats-float-deep-5: If water fills that space or the load is too great, floating can fail.
library-boats-float-deep-6: Stability matters too: an object can float but tip easily.
library-boats-float-deep-7: Our cross-section omits waves, leaks and balance changes; it is not boating or water-safety advice.
library-airplanes-tell-1: Air flows around a plane’s wings.
library-airplanes-tell-3: Air pushes the plane upward too.
library-airplanes-more-1: A plane in flight has four main forces to consider: lift, weight, thrust and drag.
library-airplanes-more-2: Wings moving through air can generate lift.
library-airplanes-more-3: An engine supplies thrust to overcome drag.
library-airplanes-more-4: In steady, level flight, lift balances weight and thrust balances drag.
library-airplanes-more-5: A plane does not stay up just because its top wing surface is curved.
library-airplanes-deep-1: Lift results from how a wing changes the airflow and pressure around it.
library-airplanes-deep-2: The wing’s shape, its angle to the oncoming air and the speed all affect lift.
library-airplanes-deep-3: Air moving around the wing is deflected, with a net downward change in momentum; the air exerts an upward reaction on the wing.
library-airplanes-deep-4: Pressure differences and flow turning describe the same interaction in related ways.
library-airplanes-deep-5: Air parcels above and below a wing do not have to reunite at the trailing edge.
library-airplanes-deep-6: Our arrows are a simplified flow model, not a flight simulation.
library-airplanes-deep-7: A safe paper drawing can compare forces without launching anything at people or trying to copy a real aircraft.
library-bicycle-tell-1: Your feet can turn the pedals.
library-bicycle-tell-2: A chain helps turn the back wheel.
library-bicycle-tell-3: The wheel pushes on the ground.
library-bicycle-more-1: On a chain-driven bicycle, pedals turn cranks and a toothed chainring.
library-bicycle-more-2: The chain passes motion to a rear sprocket and wheel.
library-bicycle-more-3: The tire pushes backward on the ground, and the ground pushes the bicycle forward.
library-bicycle-more-5: A balance bike or another kind of cycle may work differently.
library-bicycle-deep-1: A bicycle brings several mechanisms together: rotating wheels, crank levers, a chain drive and brakes.
library-bicycle-deep-2: Changing the tooth-count ratio between chainring and rear sprocket changes how many wheel turns follow a crank turn.
library-bicycle-deep-3: A lower gear can reduce pedal force on a hill at the cost of more pedal turns for a given travel distance.
library-bicycle-deep-4: The rider still supplies energy, and friction and air resistance use some of it.
library-bicycle-deep-5: Directly meshing external gears turn in opposite directions, but two sprockets connected by an ordinary uncrossed chain turn in the same direction.
library-bicycle-deep-6: This is a diagram for understanding, not riding instruction or a reason to handle a moving chain.
